questions.stem: About content words and function words:
options: Nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs are content words
Prepositions can usually be predicted from word-formation patterns
Content words form an open, ever-growing class
Pronouns, prepositions and conjunctions are function words forming a closed class
questions.explanation: Function words (pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions) form a closed class and must simply be memorised; content words can be predicted from context and word formation.
although = conjunction, in = preposition, they = pronoun. Gradually is an adverb, a content word.

questions.stem: Which forms of the same root are correctly labelled?
questions.explanation: The lecture's example of a root shifting word class: diagnose (V) → diagnosis (N) → diagnostic (Adj).

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the correct word form?
options: The diagnose was confirmed by the tests.
The diagnostic tests confirmed the diagnosis.
questions.explanation: diagnostic (adjective) modifies tests; diagnosis is the noun; diagnose is the verb. Choosing the wrong form produces an ungrammatical sentence.

questions.stem: Which nouns are uncountable according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Countable: one symptom, two symptoms. Uncountable: blood, oxygen, pain.

questions.stem: Which noun–verb pairs are correct (noun formed from the verb)?
questions.explanation: Suffixes -ment, -ion, -ing form nouns from verbs: examine → examination.

questions.stem: In which phrases is a noun used as an adjective?
questions.explanation: The first noun modifies the second (heart → failure). In "severe pain", severe is a true adjective.

questions.stem: Match each sentence to its tense as given in the lecture:
options: "The patient remains stable at the time of writing." — present
"Mr Thomas was diagnosed with Type 2 diabetes in 2019." — past
"She has been prescribed metformin 500 mg twice daily." — present perfect
questions.explanation: Tense signals past history (past), current status (present), and the present perfect links past to present.
she is a subject pronoun; the object form is her.

questions.stem: Which adjectives does the lecture list under clinical state?
questions.explanation: Clinical state: stable, deteriorating, improving, responsive, non-compliant, elevated, swollen, tender. Ambulatory is a patient descriptor.

options: They answer how, when or to what degree
questions.explanation: Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives or other adverbs. The manner and speed of onset can matter diagnostically.

questions.stem: Which verb + preposition collocations are correct?
questions.explanation: present with symptoms · suffer from · respond to · refer to · complain of.

questions.stem: Which phrase is idiomatically correct according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: English says "a pain in the chest", not "at the chest". The lecture also gives "for three days" and "on his forearm".

questions.stem: Match the conjunction to its type:
questions.explanation: Coordinating: and, but, or, so, for, nor, yet. Subordinating: because, although, since, while, when, if, unless. Correlative: both…and, either…or, neither…nor, not only…but also.

options: Connect a dependent clause to an independent clause
questions.explanation: Pairs working together are correlative conjunctions.

questions.stem: In "The experienced surgeon carefully examined the patient before surgery":
questions.explanation: examined is the verb. This is the formative assessment's sentence-analysis item.

questions.stem: Why does the lecture study only seven of the eight parts of speech?
options: Pronouns are not a part of speech
Conjunctions are covered in a later lecture
Interjections are rare in formal medical writing
questions.explanation: The eight are nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions and interjections; the lecture focuses on the first seven.
